intro: If your Jackson lawn has sprouted raised ridges and volcano-shaped mounds, you are dealing with the eastern mole (Scalopus aquaticus), the burrowing insectivore behind almost all turf tunneling in this part of the central Georgia Piedmont. Because the climate here is mild, moles never go dormant the way they do up north, so a Jackson yard can show fresh runs in January as readily as July. The fix that actually holds is trapping the runways the mole is using right now — not the repellents and sonic stakes sold for the job.
extendedBody:
What a Mole Is Doing Under Your Jackson Lawn

Moles are not after your plants. The eastern mole eats earthworms and soil grubs, and it has to take in well over half its body weight in food a day, so it tunnels constantly in search of them. That appetite is why the best-kept lawns suffer the most: a watered, healthy Jackson lawn over the area's moist Piedmont clay holds a dense earthworm population, and the mole simply follows the food. Activity tends to jump in the day or two after rain, when worms rise toward the surface and the mole pushes shallow feeding runs up to meet them.

Mole or Vole? Read the Damage First

Half of what gets called a mole problem in Jackson is actually a vole problem, and the two need opposite treatments — so identify before you act:

  • Moles push up raised ridges and cone-shaped soil mounds. The harm is mechanical: heaved, drying turf and lifted roots. No chewed plants.
  • Voles leave narrow, ground-level runways of clipped grass and pencil-width holes, with no ridges, and they gnaw roots, bulbs, and the bark of young shrubs.

Ridges and mounds point to a mole, and the rest of this page is for that animal. Surface trails through the grass mean a rodent problem handled a different way.

Clearing the Mole — and Why the Shortcuts Fail

One approach removes a mole reliably, and it is not what most homeowners try first:

  • Trap the live runs. A mole digs far more tunnel than it keeps using, so most of the runs in a yard are already abandoned. Each suspect run is tamped flat; the sections that re-raise within a day or two are the active highways, and those are where traps go. Setting on dead tunnels is the single most common reason a do-it-yourself attempt produces nothing.
  • Skip the gadgets. Castor-oil granules at best shove the animal to another corner of the lawn for a while, and vibrating stakes, ultrasonic spikes, and mothballs have never held up in university extension testing.
  • Treat grubs as a supporting move. If white grubs are feeding the problem, knocking them back makes the turf less appealing, but a mole working an earthworm supply will stay until it is trapped — grub control supports the trapping, it does not replace it.

Across Jackson's Different Lawns

The pattern shifts a little by neighborhood. The mature, long-irrigated lawns around the historic-downtown courthouse square and the older 1900s-1970s residential blocks tend to hold the steadiest earthworm populations and the most persistent runs. The newer subdivision turf on the city edges sees flushes of activity after the lawn is established and the soil life builds up. In every case the durable result comes from removing the animal on its active runways and keeping the turf monitored, since a cleared lawn next to open ground can be recolonized by a neighboring mole.

faqs.q: What does mole removal cost in Jackson?
faqs.a: Most Jackson mole jobs are priced on an initial trapping program rather than a single visit, because clearing a lawn means working the active runs until the resident mole or moles are removed. Lawn size and how many separate tunnel systems are running set the price. Ask for an estimate after a quick look at the damage pattern.

faqs.q: Why does my Jackson yard keep getting moles?
faqs.a: Because it feeds them. A healthy, watered lawn over Jackson's moist Piedmont clay supports a heavy earthworm population, and moles travel to the food. Yards that back onto open or wooded ground are also easy to recolonize once a resident mole is removed, which is why monitoring after trapping matters.

faqs.q: Do mole repellents work on a Jackson lawn?
faqs.a: Not as a fix. Castor-oil products may relocate a mole within the same yard temporarily, and sonic or vibrating stakes and mothballs have repeatedly failed in extension trials. Trapping the active runways is the only method that reliably removes the animal.

faqs.q: When are moles worst in Jackson?
faqs.a: There is no off-season here. Central Georgia's mild climate keeps moles active and tunneling year-round, and surface damage tends to spike in the day or two after rain when earthworms move up and the mole follows.

faqs.q: Are moles dangerous or will they bite?
faqs.a: Moles are not a health threat and are not aggressive — they live almost entirely underground and do not bite people or pets. The problem they cause is turf damage, not danger.
